anchors.reason: Miran argues that deregulation is a large positive supply shock that lowers prices and widens the output gap, so it "supports a more accommodative stance of monetary policy." He says policy has been "tighter than it should have been" and that he expects to press this view with FOMC colleagues, which implies a faster and larger easing path than the committee expects.

anchors.speaker: Christopher J. Waller
anchors.title: Statement by Governor Christopher J. Waller
anchors.path: After three cuts in 2025 and a hold at the January 2026 meeting, the FOMC and markets expect a pause with gradual further easing later, roughly one or two cuts in 2026.
anchors.reason: Waller dissented in favor of a 25bp cut, saying "economic data make it clear to me further easing is needed" and that policy is still 50 to 75bp above neutral. He stresses a weak labor market with "zero" 2025 job growth, a significant risk of deterioration, and tariff inflation that can be looked through. This is a clearly easier path than the committee's hold.

anchors.speaker: Michelle W. Bowman
anchors.title: Outlook for the Economy and Monetary Policy
anchors.path: As of January 2026, after three 25bp cuts to 3.50-3.75%, the FOMC is expected to pause at the late-January meeting, with perhaps one or two more cuts later in 2026.
anchors.reason: Bowman says the labor market is fragile and policy is still 'moderately restrictive.' She argues the Fed should 'remain ready to adjust policy to bring it closer to neutral' and should avoid signaling a pause, which is more dovish than the expected pause. She also sees inflation falling toward 2% once tariff effects fade, and says risks are not symmetric and tilt toward employment.

anchors.speaker: Philip N. Jefferson
anchors.title: Economic Outlook and Supply-Side (Dis)Inflation Dynamics
anchors.path: FOMC paused in late January 2026 after 175bp of cuts since mid-2024; markets expect a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting path with perhaps a couple more cuts later in 2026.
anchors.reason: Jefferson supported holding rates, says policy is 'broadly in the range of estimates of the neutral rate' and 'well positioned,' with a meeting-by-meeting, data-dependent approach. He leans slightly dovish by expecting disinflation to resume, treating tariffs as a one-time price-level shift, and saying there is 'more leeway' without 'precautionary monetary policy restraint.' He also notes that downside risks to employment remain, but acknowledges upside inflation risks and a possibly higher neutral rate.

anchors.speaker: John Williams
anchors.title: A Few Words for the New Year
anchors.path: After 75bp of cuts in 2025, the FOMC is expected to hold near-term, with perhaps one or two more cuts in 2026 as inflation peaks in H1 and the labor market stabilizes.
anchors.reason: Williams says policy is 'well positioned' after 75bp of cuts, with the stance moved 'closer to neutral' and risks 'in better balance'. He gives a favorable outlook (inflation peaking at 2-3/4 to 3 percent, then falling; unemployment stabilizing) and stays data dependent. He signals neither further cuts nor hikes.

anchors.speaker: Jerome H. Powell
anchors.title: FOMC press conference, 18 March 2026
anchors.path: Hold at 3.5-3.75% in March, with the SEP median still showing one cut in 2026 (3.4% at year-end) and another in 2027 (3.1%), conditional on tariff disinflation.
anchors.reason: Powell holds rates and leaves the median SEP path unchanged, but he leans slightly hawkish. He says the 'look through' question 'doesn't really arise until we have kind of checked that box' on tariff progress, notes movement toward fewer cuts, says a rate increase 'did come up', and says 'if we don't see that progress, then you won't see the rate cut'. He also stresses downside labor risks and says nobody knows how the oil shock will play out, which keeps the stance balanced.

anchors.speaker: Lisa D. Cook
anchors.title: Economic Outlook
anchors.path: FOMC held the policy rate steady in late January 2026 after three cuts in 2025; markets expect a pause with perhaps a couple of further cuts later in 2026, data-dependent.
anchors.reason: Cook says "I see risks as tilted toward higher inflation" and supported holding the rate until she sees "stronger evidence that inflation is moving sustainably back down to target." She also stresses credibility and dismisses weak sentiment as not signaling slack that demand-side policy can fix. She stays balanced by noting labor market risks and some optimism on inflation, and she does not call for hikes.

anchors.speaker: Beth Hammack
anchors.title: Trimming the Sails: Communicating My Reaction Function
anchors.path: The speech implies the FOMC holds a restrictive stance, with markets pricing rates on hold or modestly higher as inflation stays elevated (headline PCE 3.4%, core 3.0%).
anchors.reason: Hammack says inflation risks are skewed to the upside, pressures are broad and persistent, and an inflationary mindset may be taking hold. She sees the labor market as stable, financial conditions as neutral, and the economy as able to handle 'a tighter hand on the tiller.' She favors 'frequent smaller adjustments' and says elevated inflation could mean 'pointing the bow of monetary policy rates toward an even higher latitude.' She stops short of an explicit call for hikes, so the score is not higher.

anchors.speaker: Lorie Logan
anchors.title: Opening remarks for moderated conversation at The University of Texas at El Paso
anchors.path: FOMC and markets appear to expect policy on hold at the current rate for now, with no near-term change and no hike clearly priced in.
anchors.reason: Logan says inflation is "taking too long to return" to 2%, that it is likely trending only to the "mid 2's", and that "monetary policy is not restraining the economy." She is "increasingly concerned that higher interest rates could be necessary later this year," which is an explicit tightening bias beyond a hold. She hedges by noting that decisions call for debate and by saying she respects her colleagues' views, so the score stops short of the top of the hawkish range.

anchors.speaker: Jeff Schmid
anchors.title: Agriculture, the Economy, and the Kansas City Fed
anchors.path: The FOMC is presumed to be on hold at a roughly neutral-to-modestly-restrictive rate, with no near-term hikes priced in and inflation expected to ease gradually.
anchors.reason: Schmid says his focus is 'squarely on inflation that remains too high', dismisses the idea that supply shocks are transitory, and says he does not see policy as restrictive given strong demand. He concludes that getting inflation to 2 percent 'will require tighter policy', an explicit call for hikes beyond the expected hold.
